### The Light in Apartment 3B

Mara had started measuring her life in unopened mail.

Bills slid under her door and stayed there. Birthday cards leaned against the wall until they yellowed at the edges. A flyer for a lost cat lay face-up in the hallway for three days before she picked it up, not because she cared about the cat, but because the word **LOST** looked too much like an accusation.

She lived in Apartment 3B, above a bakery that filled the stairwell each morning with the smell of warm bread. For months, that smell had felt like proof that the world was still stubbornly continuing without her.

People at work had stopped asking if she was all right. At first, they’d tried gently—coffee invitations, “You seem tired,” a hand on her shoulder. Mara had become skilled at smiling in a way that ended conversations.

“I’m fine,” she would say.

Fine was a small, hard word. It fit easily in her mouth.

On a Thursday in November, rain scratched at the windows, and Mara sat on the kitchen floor with her back against the cabinets. The apartment around her was dim except for one lamp in the living room, its shade tilted slightly to the left. She had noticed the tilt days ago and lacked the strength to fix it.

Her phone buzzed.

She ignored it.

It buzzed again.

Then again.

Finally, irritated by the noise more than anything else, she reached for it.

**DAD**.

She let it ring until it stopped.

A moment later, a text appeared.

> Just saw a heron by the river. Remember how you used to call them “old men birds”? Made me think of you.

His notebooks were full of black ink moons, broken-winged birds, and sentences copied from songs that made grief sound like a velvet coat you could wear to look mysterious. He posted photos of empty roads at midnight and captioned them with lines like *Some people are born to disappear.*

People commented hearts.  
They called him poetic.  
They called him deep.

No one called him sick.

Lena did, but only in her head. She had known Milo since they were eight, when his hair stuck up in the back and he cried if he lost at checkers. Back then, sadness was not beautiful. It was just a boy with a trembling chin, needing someone to sit beside him.

Now, sadness had become his brand.

At lunch, Milo sat under the stairwell, sketching a person standing at the edge of a cliff.

“That’s cheerful,” Lena said, dropping her tray beside him.

Milo smirked without looking up. “It’s honest.”

“It’s dramatic.”

“Same thing.”

“No,” she said. “It isn’t.”

He finally looked at her. His eyes were tired in a way she didn’t know how to fix. “You wouldn’t get it.”

The words stung because they were partly true. Lena didn’t know what it felt like inside his head. She didn’t know why he stopped answering texts, why he slept through first period, why jokes slid off him like rain off glass.

But she knew something was wrong.

And she knew the way people praised his darkness made it worse.

That Friday, the school literary magazine published one of Milo’s poems. It was about vanishing. The comments online came fast.

*This is gorgeous.*  
*You’re such a tortured soul.*  
*I wish I could write pain like this.*  
*Tragic boys are the prettiest.*

Lena stared at the screen until the words blurred.

Then she typed: *This isn’t pretty. This sounds like someone hurting.*

She deleted it.

Then she typed again: *Milo, are you okay?*

She sent that one privately.

He didn’t answer.

That night, Lena lay awake listening to her parents watch television downstairs. Her phone rested on her chest, silent. At 1:13 a.m., it buzzed.

*Milo: do you ever think people only care when it’s too late?*

Lena sat up so fast her blanket fell to the floor.

She wanted to say something perfect. Something wise. Something that would slice through the dark and pull him back by the sleeve.

Instead, her hands shook.

*I care now,* she wrote. *Where are you?*

No answer.

She called. Once. Twice. The third time, he picked up.

For a few seconds, all she heard was wind.

“Milo?” Her voice cracked. “Talk to me.”

“I’m tired,” he said.

“I know.”

“No, you don’t.”

“You’re right,” Lena said. “I don’t. But I’m here.”

There was a long silence. She could hear him breathing, uneven and small.

“I thought it would mean something,” he whispered.

“What would?”

“If I disappeared. If everyone finally understood.”

Lena pressed her fist against her mouth, fighting panic. She remembered the hearts under his poems, the comments calling his pain beautiful, the way everyone admired the smoke and ignored the fire.

“It would mean we failed you,” she said. “It wouldn’t be beautiful, Milo. It would just be awful. It would be your mom screaming. It would be your little brother waiting for you to come home. It would be your desk empty and nobody knowing what to do with all the things they should’ve said.”

He made a sound like he was trying not to cry.

“And it wouldn’t prove your pain was real,” Lena continued. “Your pain is already real. You don’t have to die for people to believe you.”

The wind rushed again.

“I don’t know how to stay,” he said.

“Then don’t figure out forever,” Lena said. “Figure out ten minutes. Stay for ten minutes and talk to me.”

“I can’t.”

“Yes, you can. Ten minutes. Then another ten. I’ll stay too.”

This time, when he was quiet, it didn’t feel empty. It felt like someone holding onto a rope with both hands.

Lena woke her parents. Her mother called Milo’s mother. His mother called for help.

By morning, Milo was safe.

Not fixed. Not magically grateful. Not transformed by love into someone who never hurt again. Safe.

That mattered more than any poem.

When Milo returned to school two weeks later, nobody knew what to say. The same people who once called him beautifully tragic now looked away, embarrassed by the realness of him. He was thinner. Quieter. Alive.

Lena found him under the stairwell again.

He was drawing in his notebook.

“No cliffs?” she asked.

He showed her the page.

It was a sink full of dirty dishes. A pair of sneakers by a door. A cracked mug. A window with pale morning light coming through.

“It’s boring,” he said.

Lena smiled. “It’s honest.”

Milo looked down at the drawing. “My therapist says I keep making pain into something grand because it’s easier than admitting it’s ugly.”

“Pain is ugly,” Lena said. “But you aren’t.”

He swallowed and blinked hard.

It was about answering one text. It was about sitting at the kitchen table while your mother makes toast and cries when she thinks you aren’t looking.

Some people said it wasn’t as pretty as his old work.

Milo didn’t care.

At the bottom of the poem, he added one line:

*Do not make a halo out of someone’s suffering. Hold their hand instead.*

And for once, everyone read it quietly.

Not because sadness was beautiful.

Because a boy was alive to write it.

- False positive rate: bad borrowers incorrectly approved
- False negative rate: good borrowers incorrectly rejected

Your training label may reflect past lending decisions rather than true repayment ability.
